To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

students who have negative racial interactions and who strongly identify with their intended major are less likely to persist than those who have not had negative racial interactions or who do not strongly identify.

1) students who reported higher levels of negative racial interactions were less likely to persist; 2) students who reported identifying with the behavioral science domain were less likely to change majors; 3) students who reported a combination of negative racial interactions and identification with their major were less likely to continue in the biomedical science major; and 4) students who reported negative racial interactions and a combination of negative interactions and identification were less likely to remain in the behavioral science major.

(a) the combination of negative racial interactions and a science identity negatively affects underrepresented racial minorities' persistence in biomedical and behavioral science majors, and (b) the combination of these two experiences is a significant predictor of underrepresented students' persistence in their intended science major.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how racial stigmas and identity impact the persistence decisions of underrepresented racial minority students.
the role of racial stigma and science identity in predicting science persistence.
the impact of racial stigmas and science identity on persistence among biomedical and behavioral science aspirants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
racial stigma and identity are significant predictors of persistence in biomedical and behavioral science.

the combination of having a negative racial interaction experience and identifying with one of the domains of science (behavioral or biomedical) has a negative impact on the persistence of URM freshmen.

students who reported having negative racial interactions with peers or faculty in their domain of science, and also identified with their domain of study, were less likely to persist as a biomedical or behavioral science student.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

students who experience negative racial interactions are more likely to identify with science, but that this identity is negatively impacted if they are also exposed to negative interactions in their domain of study.
the combination of negative racial interactions and science identity can lead to a decrease in persistence among underrepresented racial minority students.
racial stigmas can be a barrier to success for underrepresented students in science.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of racial interactions on science persistence is not uniform.
students who have negative experiences in their science classes and who do not identify with science are less likely to persist.
the negative experiences that students of color have on campus are not isolated incidents.
